Panel (B) adapted from Figure 2 of Cavanagh et al., 2016. Panel (E) adapted from Figure 5 of Stern et al., 2021. The timescale of intrinsic fluctuations in spiking activity can be also estimated from single-neuron spike autocorrelation functions (Figure 8B). In awake head-fixed primates, during periods of ongoing activity, the distribution of intrinsic autocorrelation timescales within the same cortical circuit was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal (Figure 8B), in the range from 10 ms to 1 s (Cavanagh et al., 2016). Moreover, comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations during ongoing periods revealed a hierarchical structure across cortical areas, varying from 50 to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis (Murray et al., 2014; Figure 8C). While all these results were obtained in restrained animals, it is an open question whether neural activity during naturalistic behavior exhibits temporal hierarchies similar to those observed in behavior. Current evidence from freely moving rodents engaged in waiting tasks (Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022) revealed the presence of multiple timescales in single-neuron activity from secondary motor and prefrontal cortices. These timescales range from the sub-second scale (single attractors), to a few seconds (attractor sequences), to tens of seconds or minutes (trial history dependence). It is tantalizing to speculate that even longer timescales may be present for neural activity to be able to generate the vast hierarchy of timescales observed in naturalistic behavior (Figure 7). Evidence from associative learning tasks in rodents found that population activity in hippocampal CA1 and CA3 encodes multiplexed information about several aspects of the task occurring on multiple trials such as context, place, value, and objects (McKenzie et al., 2014). Although an explicit analysis of temporal correlations was not carried out in this study, these results suggest that a hierarchy of timescales may be present in the hippocampus and emerge during learning. ### Computational mechanisms underlying heterogeneous distributions of timescales What are the computational mechanisms underlying this hierarchical temporal structure featuring a wide distribution of timescales? Single-cell biophysical properties such as differences in membrane time constant across cell types or synaptic time constants across receptors (e.g., faster AMPA and GABA vs. slower NMDA receptors) may generate multiple timescales in sub-second range, from a few milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds (Gjorgjieva et al., 2016). Although this class of single-cell mechanisms might explain the temporal hierarchy observed in the posterior–anterior cortical axis (Murray et al., 2014) by relying on systematic differences in cell-type-specific features, they are unlikely to explain the much wider temporal hierarchy observed across neurons within the same area (Figure 8A and B), or the even larger hierarchy observed in behavior (Figure 7). Theoretical studies highlighted the central role played by recurrent synaptic couplings within a local circuit for generating long timescales emerging from the recurrent dynamics. Recurrent networks with random recurrent couplings can generate time-varying neural activity whose timescale may be tuned to very slow values at a critical point (Toyoizumi and Abbott, 2011; Magnasco et al., 2009). Long timescales may also emerge in random neural networks with an excess of symmetric couplings (Martí et al., 2018). In these examples, all cells share the same timescale. Although this common timescale can be tuned to arbitrarily long values, these circuits are incapable of giving rise to temporal heterogeneity either at the single cell or at the population level. Two biologically plausible ingredients were shown to be sufficient to generate long timescales with temporal heterogeneity in their distributions: recurrent couplings realizing local functional neural clusters and heterogeneity in synaptic couplings. The first requirement of functional assemblies is a connectivity motif ubiquitously observed in biological circuits, namely, the fact that the strength of recurrent couplings decays with spatial distance between pairs of neurons, leading to the emergence of local functional assemblies of strongly coupled neurons (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Kiani et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014). In recurrent linear network models, functional assemblies can generate neural activity exhibiting slow relaxation times following stimulation. In order to generate a heterogeneity in the distribution of relaxation times, functional assemblies can be coupled by heterogeneous long-range connections, arranged along a spatial feedforward gradient (Figure 8D; Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013; Chaudhuri et al., 2014). Linear networks featuring both local functional assemblies and spatial heterogeneity in long-range couplings were able to reproduce the heterogeneous decay times found in the brainstem oculomotor integrator circuit in zebrafish and primates (Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013) and in the reward integration times in the macaque cortex (Bernacchia et al., 2011). It remains an open question whether these integrator models could be generalized to explain hierarchical activity in motor generation, perhaps stacking multiple layers of them. A shortcoming of these models is the fact that they require fine-tuning of synaptic couplings and do not generate attractor dynamics, which recent experimental evidence suggests is the basic building block of preparatory motor activity (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022). Other network models generating multiple timescales of activity fluctuations were proposed based on self-tuned criticality with anti-Hebbian plasticity (Magnasco et al., 2009) or multiple block-structured connectivity (Aljadeff et al., 2015). An alternative robust and biologically plausible way to generate a vast hierarchy of timescales was proposed based on the ingredients of recurrent functional clusters and heterogeneity in synaptic couplings (Figure 8E; Stern et al., 2021), two common features observed across cortical circuits (Marshel et al., 2019; Kiani et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014; Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016), supported by theoretical evidence (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021). In this model, excitatory and inhibitory neurons are arranged in clusters of heterogeneous sizes, generating metastable activity whose typical timescale is measured by the on–off cluster switching time (see Appendix 3). In this model, a cluster’s timescale is proportional to its size and larger clusters exhibit longer timescales, yielding a heterogeneous distribution of timescales in the range observed in cortex (Figure 8A–C). An appealing feature of this model is that it could be generalized to other domains that exhibit fluctuations simultaneously varying over a large range of timescales, such as spin glasses (Bouchaud, 1992), metabolic networks of Escherichia coli (Almaas et al., 2004; Emmerling et al., 2002), and yeast cultures (Roussel and Lloyd, 2007; Aon et al., 2008). It remains an open question whether the relationship between a neural cluster’s size and its intrinsic timescale is realized in cortical circuits and whether it can explain the origin of the hierarchical variability in naturalistic behavior. ### Future directions: Neural mechanisms generating temporal hierarchies Future studies should address how the hierarchy of timescales found in behavior may emerge from computational mechanisms. There are several missing links along this path. First, although temporally heterogeneous neural activity was found in several brain areas and species under different experimental conditions, no study to date investigated the presence of temporal hierarchies in neural activity during naturalistic behavior. All the necessary tools are available: recent advances in neurotechnology demonstrate the feasibility of chronic recordings of large neural populations during freely moving behavior (Juavinett et al., 2019; van Daal et al., 2021); simultaneously performing behavioral classification analyses from pose tracking software (Mathis et al., 2018; Marshall et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2019). This first piece of the puzzle is thus within reach. On the theory side, although recurrent dynamics can generate heterogeneous distributions of timescales (Figure 8E), this model needs to be extended to a fully realistic framework for explaining nested temporal hierarchies in naturalistic behavior such as the proposed mesoscopic circuit in Figure 5C. Here, we propose a simple roadmap to bridge this gap, building on some of the theoretical ideas we reviewed above. This theory is based on a hierarchical structure that, for lack of a better term, we will denote ‘Attractors all the way down’ (Figure 9). We start from the observation that self-initiated actions within a behavioral sequence are represented as metastable attractors in secondary motor cortex (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022; Figure 3). We then extend this observation to a general principle positing that behavioral units at each level of the temporal hierarchy (not only actions, but also sequences, activities) are represented by metastable attractors. The stochasticity in behavioral unit duration can be achieved by generating transitions between attractors at each level via low-dimensional variability, arising from mesoscopic feedback loops involving cortex and subcortical areas (Recanatesi et al., 2022; Figure 3D). The average transition time between behavioral units at each level will then depend on the barrier height separating the corresponding attractors (Cao et al., 2016; Mazzucato et al., 2019; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021). As one moves up the hierarchy from actions (fast transitions = lower barriers) to sequences and activities (slow transitions = higher barriers), the potential wells separating the corresponding attractors become deeper and the basins of attraction wider. This increase in timescales can be achieved in a biological manner by assuming that increasingly larger neural populations encode for slower behavioral features (Stern et al., 2021; see Figure 8E), which can be realized in a biologically plausible way as a hierarchy of clusters within clusters (Schaub et al., 2015). Contextual modulations in average duration of a behavioral unit at each level of the hierarchy can be implemented by top-down changes of the barrier heights between attractors via gain modulation (Figure 4C). The new theoretical ingredient required for this theory to work is the presence of a nested structure in the attractor landscape, whereas the basin of attraction of lower-level attractors (actions) is contained within the basins of higher level attractors (sequences) all the way up to the largest basins representing long-term activities. The architecture of this model provides some immediate predictions for neural activity. First, neurons exhibit conjunctive selectivity to multiple variables at different levels of the hierarchy, which has been observed, for example, in rodent hippocampus during freely moving tasks (McKenzie et al., 2014) and in primate prefrontal cortex during complex decision-making tasks (Rigotti et al., 2013). Second, single-cell activity is modulated by many attractors, in agreement with the multistable activity observed in sensory (Mazzucato et al., 2015) and frontal areas (Recanatesi et al., 2022) where neuronal representations of attractors are dense rather than sparse. Third, fluctuations in the activity of single neurons should vary over multiple timescales simultaneously, encoding information about multiple levels of the hierarchy; this is the structure that was observed in C. elegans where neurons representing movements exhibit both fast and for slow fluctuations correlated to multiple levels of the behavioral hierarchy (Kaplan et al., 2020; Figure 6). ![Figure 9.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/76577/elife-76577-fig9-v1.jpg) **Figure 9.:** A computational framework to explain the hierarchical structure of behavior was discovered in the fruit fly and rodents (Figure 7). Attractors encoding for actions, sequences, and activities (left) are supported by nested basins of attractions (right), where the size of a basin determines the intrinsic timescale of the corresponding activity. Actions have small basins, corresponding to fast timescales, while activities have large basins, corresponding to slow timescales. Attractors are nonoverlapping, consistent with the tree-like structure of the behavioral hierarchy. Which network architectures can implement a hierarchical attractor landscape? The behavioral hierarchy discovered in flies (Berman et al., 2016) can be approximated as a tree: behavioral units at a lower level of the hierarchy only occur during a specific unit at a higher level of the hierarchy (Figure 7). For example, movements occurring during the fruit fly locomotion activities never occur during idle activities. This structure is typical of phylogenetic classification in taxonomy, where the distance from the root to the leaves is the same for every leaf and the tree is called ultrametric (Rammal et al., 1986). It is not known whether behavioral trees are ultrametric; in order to clarify this structure, a notion of distance in behavioral space will have to be introduced and examined. A classic model of hierarchical attractors, which could potentially capture the tree-based hierarchy, is an extension of the Hopfield network where the stored pattern is hierarchically arranged into a tree (Parga and Virasoro, 1986; Figure 9). This class of models was originally proposed to explain the effect of word semantic categorization during memory encoding, storage, and retrieval. A contamination between the domains of naturalistic behavior and natural language processing has been proposed early on (Dawkins, 1976) and recently applied to describe C. elegans (Gomez-Marin et al., 2016; Gupta and Gomez-Marin, 2019) and larval zebrafish behavior (Reddy et al., 2022). It is still an open question to determine the precise structure of the behavioral hierarchy in mammals. The results of Marshall et al., 2021 seem to suggest that the hierarchy in rats may not be tree-like as the one observed in flies (Berman et al., 2016). However, the analysis of the rodent behavior in Marshall et al., 2021 lacked the information bottleneck step, which was crucial to infer the structure of the fly hierarchy at long timescale. On general grounds, it would be interesting to investigate whether the mammalian hierarchical motor system allows for flexible and adaptable behaviors, by utilizing the same motor elements across different sequences in a hierarchical manner, as represented in the mesoscopic circuit models of Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco and Escola, 2020; Logiaco et al., 2021 (see Figure 5) and suggested by experimental evidence in Geddes et al., 2018. This flexible hierarchy could be realized by overlapping branches and would be different from the tree-like structure found in the fly. Are the computational mechanisms generating the tree-like hierarchy sufficient to generate flexible hierarchies? Recent theoretical work highlighted the importance of a neural circuit architecture that segregates the motor preparation and execution in different areas. In the cortico–thalamic–basal ganglia model of Figure 5B, flexible sequences can be generated by rearranging existing motifs as well as by learning new motifs without interfering with previous ones (Logiaco et al., 2021). Moreover, flexible sequences can be learned using biologically plausible Hebbian plasticity in the striatum (Murray and Escola, 2017). These theoretical models provide an exciting blueprint for further investigation into learning and expression of flexible behavioral hierarchies. What are potential neural implementations of this network architecture? In the case of mammals, at the lowest level of the hierarchy, neural populations in the rodent secondary motor cortex (M2) generate metastable attractors representing upcoming actions (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022). Other subcortical areas, such as the basal ganglia or the thalamus, are likely involved in the generation of complex behavioral sequences (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022). How are higher-order behavioral units, such as sequences and activities, encoded? One possibility is that they could also be encoded in M2 attractors as recent evidence suggests M2 populations encode for a wide range of behavioral variables (Cazettes et al., 2021). We hypothesize an architecture featuring nested assemblies where larger populations, whose activity varies over progressively slower timescales (Stern et al., 2021; Schaub et al., 2015), hierarchically encode for slower features of behavior (from actions to sequences to activities). Experimental evidence shows that single neurons in M2 are selective to multiple actions (Recanatesi et al., 2022), suggesting that mixed selectivity (Rigotti et al., 2013) could play an important role in generating the high-dimensional hierarchical attractor landscape necessary to capture the complexity of naturalistic behavior. An alternative architecture might involve a distributed cortical circuit where the neural representations of behavioral units at different levels of the hierarchy are encoded in multiple frontal cortical areas, such as action sequences in M2, and activities in prefrontal cortex, which is known to control behavior on longer timescales such as trial history effects (Murakami et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021). In both scenarios, we hypothesize that while behavioral units are encoded as cortical attractors, transitions between attractor rely on feedback loops involving cortico–subcortical circuits (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022). #### Behavioral energy landscape The structure of naturalistic behavior emerging on long timescales in the fruit fly is a hierarchical tree-like organization (Figure 7A), which is consistent with an underlying neural circuit architecture based on hierarchical basins of attractions (Figure 9). Can we derive a representation of behavior as a complex energy landscape directly from the behavioral data itself? A promising approach is given by the probability density map approach (Berman et al., 2016). One could define the log-probability of the density map as an energy potential, where the transition rates between behavioral features yield a probability flux along this potential landscape. It is tantalizing to speculate that using the combination of energy gradient and probability flux one could derive a data-driven nonlinear dynamical system describing behavior (Wang, 2015). Other approaches to infer a potential energy landscape directly from data have been successfully applied to spike trains (Genkin and Engel, 2020; Duncker et al., 2019), although in a regime where the energy landscape has only a few minima. Alternatively, in chemical kinetics or fluid flow, methods based on the transfer operator formalism have been applied to find effective free energy landscapes and metastable states from experimental data or simulations (Bowman et al., 2013), and have been recently applied to animal behavior (Costa et al., 2021). #### Neural mechanisms of flexible behavioral hierarchies The model of nested basins of attractions proposed in Figure 9 can explain a tree-like behavioral hierarchy, where behavioral units at lower levels (e.g., actions) are not shared by different units at a higher level (e.g., sequences), as observed in fruit flies (Berman et al., 2016). Although the tree-like hierarchical organization emerged from assays where individual animals were monitored in isolation, recent studies of social behavior seem to challenge this structure. A large variety of qualitatively new behaviors arise from social interactions, including fighting, mating, and others. While some of these behaviors involve specialized behavioral units, others involve simultaneous execution of multiple behavioral units leading to multitasking. For example, during courtship, a male fly can simultaneously approach a female fly (locomotion) and sing, two behaviors that would be mutually exclusive in the absence of a female fly. As a consequence, the simple tree-like hierarchical organization of behavior observed in isolated individuals (Figure 8) might break down during social interactions and lead to a flexible organization where actions are shared between multiple sequences and activities.

claims.source: After a rewarded trial, mice exhibited longer latency to initiate the next trial, but shorter press durations; after a failure, the opposite behavior occurred, with shorter latency to engage and longer press durations.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from the cited study.

claims.claim: Trial history effects rely on frontal areas such as medial prefrontal and secondary motor cortices.
claims.source: Inactivation experiments showed that these effects rely on frontal areas such as medial prefrontal and secondary motor cortices (Murakami et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to inactivation experiments.

claims.claim: Changes in baseline levels modulate the average transition times between metastable attractors.
claims.source: In a recurrent circuit exhibiting attractor dynamics, changes in baseline levels modulate the average transition times between metastable attractors (Mazzucato et al., 2019; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical modeling work.

claims.claim: Changes in input baseline that decrease the barrier height lead to faster transitions to the coding attractor.
claims.source: Changes in input baseline that decrease (increase) the barrier height lead to faster (slower) transitions to the coding attractor, in turn modulating reaction times.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a mechanism from the theoretical model.

claims.claim: This biologically plausible computational mechanism was proposed to explain the acceleration of sensory coding observed when gustatory stimuli are expected compared to when they are delivered as a surprise.
claims.source: This biologically plausible computational mechanism was proposed to explain the acceleration of sensory coding observed when gustatory stimuli are expected compared to when they are delivered as a surprise (Samuelsen et al., 2012; Mazzucato et al., 2019); and the faster encoding of visual stimuli observed in V1 populations during locomotion periods compared to when the mouse sits still (Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and modeling work.

claims.claim: Gain modulation is a general mechanism to flexibly control network activity in recurrent network models of motor cortex.
claims.source: Theoretical work has established gain modulation as a general mechanism to flexibly control network activity in recurrent network models of motor cortex (Stroud et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claims.claim: Individual modulation of each neuron's gain can allow a recurrent network to learn a variety of target outputs through reward-based training.
claims.source: Individual modulation of each neuron's gain can allow a recurrent network to learn a variety of target outputs through reward-based training and combine learned modulatory gain patterns to generate new movements.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited theoretical work.

claims.claim: A comparison of monocular and binocular mice revealed different visually guided strategies mice may use to perform a successful jump.
claims.source: For example, in a distance estimation task where mice were trained to jump across a variable gap, a comparison of monocular and binocular mice revealed the different visually guided strategies mice may use to perform a successful jump.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claims.claim: Mice performed more vertical head movements under monocular conditions compared to control, revealing a reliance on motion parallax cues.
claims.source: Mice performed more vertical head movements under monocular conditions compared to control (Figure 5A, states 2 and 3 occur more frequently in the monocular condition), revealing a reliance on motion parallax cues (Parker et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 5A showing the data.

claims.claim: Experimentally controlled manipulations can lead to strong changes in ongoing behavior reflected both in changes of state usage and of transition probabilities between actions.
claims.source: Experimentally controlled manipulations can lead to strong changes in ongoing behavior reflected both in changes of state usage and of transition probabilities between actions, resulting in different repertoires of behavioral sequences.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a general observation from experimental studies.

claims.claim: A classification analysis predicted with high accuracy which drug and specific dose was administered to mice from a large panel of compounds at multiple doses.
claims.source: In the latter study, a classification analysis predicted with high accuracy which drug and specific dose was administered to the mice from a large panel of compounds at multiple doses.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited study.

claims.claim: In a model of sequence generation, the basal ganglia sequentially disinhibit motif-specific thalamic units, which in turn trigger motif preparation and execution via a thalamocortical loop with the primary motor cortex.
claims.source: In this model (Figure 5B), the basal ganglia sequentially disinhibit motif-specific thalamic units, which in turn trigger motif preparation and execution via a thalamocortical loop with the primary motor cortex (M1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a feature of the cited model and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Sequential activity patterns can be learned in an all-inhibitory circuit representing the striatum based on biologically plausible synaptic plasticity rules.
claims.source: Within the framework of corticostriatal circuits, sequential activity patterns can be learned in an all-inhibitory circuit representing the striatum (Murray and Escola, 2017). Learning in this model is based on biologically plausible synaptic plasticity rules, consistent with the decoupling of learning and execution suggested by lesion studies showing that cortical circuits are necessary for learning, but that subcortical circuits are sufficient for expression of learned behaviors (Kawai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling and experimental work.

claims.claim: The combination of fast cortical learning and slow subcortical learning may give rise to a covert learning process through which control of behavior is gradually transferred from cortical to subcortical circuits.
claims.source: The combination of fast cortical learning and slow subcortical learning may give rise to a covert learning process through which control of behavior is gradually transferred from cortical to subcortical circuits, while protecting learned behaviors that are practiced repeatedly against overwriting by future learning.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited theoretical work.

claims.claim: In the Marshmallow task about 10% of the temporal variability in waiting times could be attributed to a trial history effect.
claims.source: For example, in the Marshmallow task about 10% of the temporal variability in waiting times could be attributed to a trial history effect, which relied on an intact medial prefrontal cortex and was abolished with its inactivation (Murakami et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: The remaining 90% of the unexplained across-repetition variability was attributed to a stochastic mechanism, likely originating from metastable dynamics.
claims.source: The remaining 90% of the unexplained across-repetition variability was attributed to a stochastic mechanism, likely originating from metastable dynamics (Recanatesi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claims.claim: The worm locomotor behavior exhibits a clear hierarchical organization with three distinct timescales: sub-second body-bends and head-casts, second-long crawling undulations, and slow reverse-forward cycles.
claims.source: The worm locomotor behavior exhibits a clear hierarchical organization with three distinct timescales: sub-second body-bends and head-casts, second-long crawling undulations, and slow reverse-forward cycles (Gomez-Marin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: At the neuronal level, the hierarchy in C. elegans is generated by nested neuronal dynamics where upper-level motor programs are supported by slow activity spread across many neurons, while lower-level behaviors are represented by fast local dynamics in small multifunctional populations.
claims.source: At the neuronal level, this hierarchy is generated by nested neuronal dynamics where upper-level motor programs are supported by slow activity spread across many neurons, while lower-level behaviors are represented by fast local dynamics in small multifunctional populations (Kaplan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Persistent activity driving higher-level behaviors gates faster activity driving lower-level behaviors in C. elegans.
claims.source: Persistent activity driving higher-level behaviors gates faster activity driving lower-level behaviors, such that, at lower levels, neurons show dynamics spanning multiple timescales simultaneously (Hallinen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: The motor hierarchy in C. elegans has a nonoverlapping, tree-like structure, in which no lower-level state is connected to multiple upper-level states.
claims.source: Specific lower-level behaviors may only be accessed via switches at upper levels, generating a nonoverlapping, tree-like hierarchy, in which no lower-level state is connected to multiple upper-level states.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the C. elegans motor hierarchy.

claims.claim: The state-level hierarchy in C. elegans may rely on neuromodulation.
claims.source: Whereas the motor hierarchy is directly generated by neuronal activity, this state-level hierarchy may rely on neuromodulation (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Flavell et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Berman et al. mapped the entire behavioral space of freely moving flies, identifying a hundred stereotyped, frequently reoccurring actions, interspersed with bouts of nonstereotyped behaviors.
claims.source: By analyzing videos of ground-based fruit fly during long sessions of spontaneous behavior (Figure 2B), Berman et al., 2014 and Berman et al., 2016 mapped the entire behavioral space of freely moving flies, identifying a hundred stereotyped, frequently reoccurring actions, interspersed with bouts of nonstereotyped behaviors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the cited studies.

claims.claim: The information bottleneck method revealed multiple timescales in the fly behavior, organized into a hierarchical structure reflecting the underlying behavioral programs and internal states.
claims.source: This predictive algorithm revealed multiple timescales in the fly behavior, organized into a hierarchical structure reflecting the underlying behavioral programs and internal states.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from applying the information bottleneck method.

claims.claim: A strongly non-Markovian structure emerges on longer timescales in fly behavior.
claims.source: These longer timescales manifest as nested blocks in the transition probability matrix, implying that a strongly non-Markovian structure emerges on longer timescales (Alba et al., 2020; Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The different branches of the fly behavioral hierarchy are segregated into a tree-like, nonoverlapping structure.
claims.source: A hallmark of the fly behavior emerging from this analysis is that the different branches of this hierarchy are segregated into a tree-like, nonoverlapping structure: for example, actions occurring during grooming do not occur during locomotion.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the analysis of fly behavior.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of single descending neurons in the fly drove stereotyped behaviors that were shared by multiple neurons and often depended on the behavioral state prior to activation.
claims.source: Optogenetic activation of single neurons during spontaneous behavior revealed that most of the descending neurons drove stereotyped behaviors that where shared by multiple neurons and often depended on the behavioral state prior to activation (Cande et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Individual flies vary considerably in the high-level temporal structure of locomotion, and in how this usage is modulated by different odors.
claims.source: An alternative statistical approach based on a hierarchical HMM revealed that, although all flies use the same set of low-level locomotor features, individual flies vary considerably in the high-level temporal structure of locomotion, and in how this usage is modulated by different odors (Tao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Behavioral idiosyncrasy of individual-to-individual phenotypic variability has been traced back to specific genes regulating neural activity in the central complex of the fly brain.
claims.source: This behavioral idiosyncrasy of individual-to-individual phenotypic variability has been traced back to specific genes (Ayroles et al., 2014) regulating neural activity (Buchanan et al., 2015) in the central complex of the fly brain.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Mice acquired the 'penguin dance' sequence hierarchically rather than sequentially, a learning scheme that is inconsistent with the classic reinforcement learning paradigm.
claims.source: Mice acquired the sequence hierarchically rather than sequentially, a learning scheme that is inconsistent with the classic reinforcement learning paradigm, which predicts sequence learning occurs in the reverse order of execution (Sutton and Barto, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding that contradicts a theoretical prediction.

claims.claim: Striatal direct and indirect pathways play differential roles in controlling the expression of a single action or a fast switch from one subsequence to the next.
claims.source: Using closed-loop optogenetic stimulation, the authors revealed the differential roles played by striatal direct and indirect pathways in controlling, respectively, the expression of a single action (either L or R), or a fast switch from one subsequence to the next (from the LL block to RR, and from RR to the reward approach).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from optogenetic manipulation.

claims.claim: Signature of non-Markovian dynamics in rat behavior peaked at 10–100 s timescales.
claims.source: Examining the behavioral transition matrix at different timescales, signature of non-Markovian dynamics peaked at 10–100 s timescales.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of rat behavior.

claims.claim: On 15 s timescales, pattern sequences emerged featuring sequentially ordered actions, such as grooming sequences of the face followed by the body.
claims.source: On 15 s timescales, pattern sequences emerged featuring sequentially ordered actions, such as grooming sequences of the face followed by the body.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of rat behavior.

claims.claim: On minute-long timescales, states of varying arousal or task engagement emerged, lacking stereotyped sequential ordering.
claims.source: On minute-long timescales, states of varying arousal or task engagement emerged, lacking stereotyped sequential ordering.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of rat behavior.

claims.claim: In a rat model of the fragile X syndrome, mutant rats showed abnormally long grooming epochs, characterized by different behavioral sequences and states compared to wildtypes.
claims.source: In a rat model of the fragile X syndrome, while mutant and wildtype rats had similar locomotor behavior, the former showed abnormally long grooming epochs, characterized by different behavioral sequences and states compared to wildtypes (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7C showing the data.

claims.claim: Differences between individual rats were more pronounced at longer timescales compared to short ones.
claims.source: Another benefit of this multiscale approach is to allow the investigation of the individuality of rodent behavior, revealing that, although all animals drew from a common set of temporal patterns, differences between individual rats were more pronounced at longer timescales compared to short ones (Marshall et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales of neural activity was found in the brainstem of the restrained larval zebrafish by measuring the decay time constant of persistent firing.
claims.source: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales of neural activity was found in the brainstem of the restrained larval zebrafish by measuring the decay time constant of persistent firing across a population of neurons comprising the oculomotor velocity-to-position neural integrator (Figure 8A; Miri et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 8A.

claims.claim: The decay times varied over a vast range 0.5–50 s across cells in individual zebrafish larvae.
claims.source: The decay times varied over a vast range 0.5–50 s across cells in individual larvae.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the cited study.

claims.claim: This heterogeneous distribution of timescales was confirmed in the primate oculomotor brainstem.
claims.source: This heterogeneous distribution of timescales was later confirmed in the primate oculomotor brainstem (Joshua et al., 2013), suggesting that timescale heterogeneity is a common feature of oculomotor integrators conserved across phylogeny.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Temporal traces of the reward delivered in previous trials were encoded in single-neuron spiking activity in frontal areas over a wide range of timescales, obeying a power law distribution up to 10 consecutive trials.
claims.source: In head-fixed monkeys performing a competitive game task, temporal traces of the reward delivered in previous trials were encoded in single-neuron spiking activity in frontal areas over a wide range of timescales, obeying a power law distribution up to 10 consecutive trials (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: The distribution of intrinsic autocorrelation timescales within the same cortical circuit was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal, in the range from 10 ms to 1 s.
claims.source: In awake head-fixed primates, during periods of ongoing activity, the distribution of intrinsic autocorrelation timescales within the same cortical circuit was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal (Figure 8B), in the range from 10 ms to 1 s (Cavanagh et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations during ongoing periods revealed a hierarchical structure across cortical areas, varying from 50 to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis.
claims.source: Moreover, comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations during ongoing periods revealed a hierarchical structure across cortical areas, varying from 50 to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis (Murray et al., 2014; Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Current evidence from freely moving rodents engaged in waiting tasks revealed the presence of multiple timescales in single-neuron activity from secondary motor and prefrontal cortices.
claims.source: While all these results were obtained in restrained animals, it is an open question whether neural activity during naturalistic behavior exhibits temporal hierarchies similar to those observed in behavior. Current evidence from freely moving rodents engaged in waiting tasks (Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022) revealed the presence of multiple timescales in single-neuron activity from secondary motor and prefrontal cortices.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: These timescales range from the sub-second scale (single attractors), to a few seconds (attractor sequences), to tens of seconds or minutes (trial history dependence).
claims.source: These timescales range from the sub-second scale (single attractors), to a few seconds (attractor sequences), to tens of seconds or minutes (trial history dependence).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the timescales observed in the cited studies.

claims.claim: Population activity in hippocampal CA1 and CA3 encodes multiplexed information about several aspects of the task occurring on multiple trials such as context, place, value, and objects.
claims.source: Evidence from associative learning tasks in rodents found that population activity in hippocampal CA1 and CA3 encodes multiplexed information about several aspects of the task occurring on multiple trials such as context, place, value, and objects (McKenzie et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Single-cell biophysical properties such as differences in membrane time constant across cell types or synaptic time constants across receptors may generate multiple timescales in sub-second range.
claims.source: Single-cell biophysical properties such as differences in membrane time constant across cell types or synaptic time constants across receptors (e.g., faster AMPA and GABA vs. slower NMDA receptors) may generate multiple timescales in sub-second range, from a few milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds (Gjorgjieva et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claims.claim: Recurrent networks with random recurrent couplings can generate time-varying neural activity whose timescale may be tuned to very slow values at a critical point.
claims.source: Recurrent networks with random recurrent couplings can generate time-varying neural activity whose timescale may be tuned to very slow values at a critical point (Toyoizumi and Abbott, 2011; Magnasco et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: Long timescales may also emerge in random neural networks with an excess of symmetric couplings.
claims.source: Long timescales may also emerge in random neural networks with an excess of symmetric couplings (Martí et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claims.claim: Two biologically plausible ingredients were shown to be sufficient to generate long timescales with temporal heterogeneity in their distributions: recurrent couplings realizing local functional neural clusters and heterogeneity in synaptic couplings.
claims.source: Two biologically plausible ingredients were shown to be sufficient to generate long timescales with temporal heterogeneity in their distributions: recurrent couplings realizing local functional neural clusters and heterogeneity in synaptic couplings.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a theoretical finding.

claims.claim: The strength of recurrent couplings decays with spatial distance between pairs of neurons, leading to the emergence of local functional assemblies of strongly coupled neurons.
claims.source: The first requirement of functional assemblies is a connectivity motif ubiquitously observed in biological circuits, namely, the fact that the strength of recurrent couplings decays with spatial distance between pairs of neurons, leading to the emergence of local functional assemblies of strongly coupled neurons (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Kiani et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Linear networks featuring both local functional assemblies and spatial heterogeneity in long-range couplings were able to reproduce the heterogeneous decay times found in the brainstem oculomotor integrator circuit in zebrafish and primates.
claims.source: Linear networks featuring both local functional assemblies and spatial heterogeneity in long-range couplings were able to reproduce the heterogeneous decay times found in the brainstem oculomotor integrator circuit in zebrafish and primates (Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013) and in the reward integration times in the macaque cortex (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling work that reproduced experimental findings.

claims.claim: In a model based on excitatory and inhibitory neurons arranged in clusters of heterogeneous sizes, a cluster's timescale is proportional to its size and larger clusters exhibit longer timescales.
claims.source: In this model, a cluster's timescale is proportional to its size and larger clusters exhibit longer timescales, yielding a heterogeneous distribution of timescales in the range observed in cortex (Figure 8A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a feature of the model described in the cited work.

claims.claim: No study to date investigated the presence of temporal hierarchies in neural activity during naturalistic behavior.
claims.source: First, although temporally heterogeneous neural activity was found in several brain areas and species under different experimental conditions, no study to date investigated the presence of temporal hierarchies in neural activity during naturalistic behavior.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a gap in the current literature.

claims.claim: Recent advances in neurotechnology demonstrate the feasibility of chronic recordings of large neural populations during freely moving behavior.
claims.source: All the necessary tools are available: recent advances in neurotechnology demonstrate the feasibility of chronic recordings of large neural populations during freely moving behavior (Juavinett et al., 2019; van Daal et al., 2021); simultaneously performing behavioral classification analyses from pose tracking software (Mathis et al., 2018; Marshall et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claims.claim: Self-initiated actions within a behavioral sequence are represented as metastable attractors in secondary motor cortex.
claims.source: We start from the observation that self-initiated actions within a behavioral sequence are represented as metastable attractors in secondary motor cortex (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Behavioral units at each level of the temporal hierarchy (actions, sequences, activities) are represented by metastable attractors.
claims.source: We then extend this observation to a general principle positing that behavioral units at each level of the temporal hierarchy (not only actions, but also sequences, activities) are represented by metastable attractors.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposed general principle extending from experimental observations.

claims.claim: The stochasticity in behavioral unit duration can be achieved by generating transitions between attractors at each level via low-dimensional variability, arising from mesoscopic feedback loops involving cortex and subcortical areas.
claims.source: The stochasticity in behavioral unit duration can be achieved by generating transitions between attractors at each level via low-dimensional variability, arising from mesoscopic feedback loops involving cortex and subcortical areas (Recanatesi et al., 2022; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The average transition time between behavioral units at each level depends on the barrier height separating the corresponding attractors.
claims.source: The average transition time between behavioral units at each level will then depend on the barrier height separating the corresponding attractors (Cao et al., 2016; Mazzucato et al., 2019; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: As one moves up the hierarchy from actions to sequences to activities, the potential wells separating the corresponding attractors become deeper and the basins of attraction wider.
claims.source: As one moves up the hierarchy from actions (fast transitions = lower barriers) to sequences and activities (slow transitions = higher barriers), the potential wells separating the corresponding attractors become deeper and the basins of attraction wider.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a feature of the proposed hierarchical model.

claims.claim: This increase in timescales can be achieved in a biological manner by assuming that increasingly larger neural populations encode for slower behavioral features.
claims.source: This increase in timescales can be achieved in a biological manner by assuming that increasingly larger neural populations encode for slower behavioral features (Stern et al., 2021; see Figure 8E), which can be realized in a biologically plausible way as a hierarchy of clusters within clusters (Schaub et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: Contextual modulations in average duration of a behavioral unit at each level of the hierarchy can be implemented by top-down changes of the barrier heights between attractors via gain modulation.
claims.source: Contextual modulations in average duration of a behavioral unit at each level of the hierarchy can be implemented by top-down changes of the barrier heights between attractors via gain modulation (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Neurons exhibit conjunctive selectivity to multiple variables at different levels of the hierarchy.
claims.source: First, neurons exhibit conjunctive selectivity to multiple variables at different levels of the hierarchy, which has been observed, for example, in rodent hippocampus during freely moving tasks (McKenzie et al., 2014) and in primate prefrontal cortex during complex decision-making tasks (Rigotti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Single-cell activity is modulated by many attractors, in agreement with the multistable activity observed in sensory and frontal areas.
claims.source: Second, single-cell activity is modulated by many attractors, in agreement with the multistable activity observed in sensory (Mazzucato et al., 2015) and frontal areas (Recanatesi et al., 2022) where neuronal representations of attractors are dense rather than sparse.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Fluctuations in the activity of single neurons should vary over multiple timescales simultaneously, encoding information about multiple levels of the hierarchy.
claims.source: Third, fluctuations in the activity of single neurons should vary over multiple timescales simultaneously, encoding information about multiple levels of the hierarchy; this is the structure that was observed in C. elegans where neurons representing movements exhibit both fast and for slow fluctuations correlated to multiple levels of the behavioral hierarchy (Kaplan et al., 2020; Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a prediction that is supported by observations in C. elegans.

claims.claim: The behavioral hierarchy discovered in flies can be approximated as a tree where behavioral units at a lower level of the hierarchy only occur during a specific unit at a higher level of the hierarchy.
claims.source: The behavioral hierarchy discovered in flies (Berman et al., 2016) can be approximated as a tree: behavioral units at a lower level of the hierarchy only occur during a specific unit at a higher level of the hierarchy (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the fly behavioral hierarchy.

claims.claim: Movements occurring during the fruit fly locomotion activities never occur during idle activities.
claims.source: For example, movements occurring during the fruit fly locomotion activities never occur during idle activities.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an example of the tree-like structure.

claims.claim: A classic model of hierarchical attractors is an extension of the Hopfield network where the stored pattern is hierarchically arranged into a tree.
claims.source: A classic model of hierarchical attractors, which could potentially capture the tree-based hierarchy, is an extension of the Hopfield network where the stored pattern is hierarchically arranged into a tree (Parga and Virasoro, 1986; Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claims.claim: This class of models was originally proposed to explain the effect of word semantic categorization during memory encoding, storage, and retrieval.
claims.source: This class of models was originally proposed to explain the effect of word semantic categorization during memory encoding, storage, and retrieval.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the original application of the model.

claims.claim: The results of Marshall et al., 2021 suggest that the hierarchy in rats may not be tree-like as the one observed in flies.
claims.source: It is still an open question to determine the precise structure of the behavioral hierarchy in mammals. The results of Marshall et al., 2021 seem to suggest that the hierarchy in rats may not be tree-like as the one observed in flies (Berman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental findings.

claims.claim: The mammalian hierarchical motor system may allow for flexible and adaptable behaviors, by utilizing the same motor elements across different sequences in a hierarchical manner.
claims.source: On general grounds, it would be interesting to investigate whether the mammalian hierarchical motor system allows for flexible and adaptable behaviors, by utilizing the same motor elements across different sequences in a hierarchical manner, as represented in the mesoscopic circuit models of Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco and Escola, 2020; Logiaco et al., 2021 (see Figure 5) and suggested by experimental evidence in Geddes et al., 2018.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to modeling and experimental work.

claims.claim: In the cortico–thalamic–basal ganglia model, flexible sequences can be generated by rearranging existing motifs as well as by learning new motifs without interfering with previous ones.
claims.source: In the cortico–thalamic–basal ganglia model of Figure 5B, flexible sequences can be generated by rearranging existing motifs as well as by learning new motifs without interfering with previous ones (Logiaco et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claims.claim: Flexible sequences can be learned using biologically plausible Hebbian plasticity in the striatum.
claims.source: Moreover, flexible sequences can be learned using biologically plausible Hebbian plasticity in the striatum (Murray and Escola, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claims.claim: At the lowest level of the hierarchy, neural populations in the rodent secondary motor cortex (M2) generate metastable attractors representing upcoming actions.
claims.source: In the case of mammals, at the lowest level of the hierarchy, neural populations in the rodent secondary motor cortex (M2) generate metastable attractors representing upcoming actions (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Other subcortical areas, such as the basal ganglia or the thalamus, are likely involved in the generation of complex behavioral sequences.
claims.source: Other subcortical areas, such as the basal ganglia or the thalamus, are likely involved in the generation of complex behavioral sequences (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling and experimental work.

claims.claim: Single neurons in M2 are selective to multiple actions, suggesting that mixed selectivity could play an important role in generating the high-dimensional hierarchical attractor landscape necessary to capture the complexity of naturalistic behavior.
claims.source: Experimental evidence shows that single neurons in M2 are selective to multiple actions (Recanatesi et al., 2022), suggesting that mixed selectivity (Rigotti et al., 2013) could play an important role in generating the high-dimensional hierarchical attractor landscape necessary to capture the complexity of naturalistic behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work and theoretical concepts.

claims.claim: While behavioral units are encoded as cortical attractors, transitions between attractor rely on feedback loops involving cortico–subcortical circuits.
claims.source: In both scenarios, we hypothesize that while behavioral units are encoded as cortical attractors, transitions between attractor rely on feedback loops involving cortico–subcortical circuits (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to modeling work.

claims.claim: During courtship, a male fly can simultaneously approach a female fly (locomotion) and sing, two behaviors that would be mutually exclusive in the absence of a female fly.
claims.source: For example, during courtship, a male fly can simultaneously approach a female fly (locomotion) and sing, two behaviors that would be mutually exclusive in the absence of a female fly.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an example of multitasking during social behavior.

claims.claim: The simple tree-like hierarchical organization of behavior observed in isolated individuals might break down during social interactions and lead to a flexible organization where actions are shared between multiple sequences and activities.
claims.source: As a consequence, the simple tree-like hierarchical organization of behavior observed in isolated individuals (Figure 8) might break down during social interactions and lead to a flexible organization where actions are shared between multiple sequences and activities.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis about how social interactions may change behavioral organization.

results.result: Naturalistic animal behavior exhibits temporal variability arising from three sources: hierarchical (actions nested into sequences into activities), contextual (e.g., expectation effects), and stochastic (right-skewed duration distributions). This hierarchical organization is ubiquitously observed across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the foundational framework of the review, supported by citations to foundational theoretical work (C3) and stated as established observations (C4). The three-axis decomposition is explicitly stated in the abstract and introduction with supporting evidence from figures and prior literature.

results.result: The review proposes metastable attractors as a unifying mechanistic principle for temporal variability in behavior. Transitions between attractors are driven by internally generated neural variability, can be regulated by single-cell gain modulation, and hierarchies of timescales emerge from heterogeneous neural cluster sizes.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 outline the core theoretical framework reviewed in the manuscript. C8 is supported by citation (La Camera et al., 2019), while C9-C11 represent the main theoretical contributions reviewed. These are presented as established findings from the cited literature and form the mechanistic basis of the review.

results.result: Recent computational methods for pose tracking have revolutionized behavioral analysis across species. At action timescales, transition times follow Poisson processes with right-skewed distributions, though state-space models fail to capture longer timescale non-Markovian structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are well-supported by multiple citations to methodological advances. C14 is supported by citation and Figure 3. C15 acknowledges a limitation of current models, which is appropriate for a review article identifying gaps in the field.

results.result: The secondary motor cortex (M2) in rodents is involved in motor planning and action timing. Ensemble activity in M2 unfolds via sequences of multineuron-firing patterns lasting hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, with specific patterns reliably preceding self-initiated actions. These patterns may represent attractors of recurrent circuit dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are supported by multiple citations to experimental work and Figure 3 data. C19 is stated as a hypothesis based on observations. C20 provides a definition. C21 is supported by citation to experimental work (Inagaki et al., 2019). The progression from experimental observation to theoretical interpretation is appropriate.

results.result: Attractors can be stable or metastable. M2 ensemble activity during the Marshmallow task is consistent with metastable attractor sequences, where attractor onset drives action initiation and dwell time sets inter-action intervals. A two-area mesoscopic network model with M2 and subcortical areas explains the observed dynamics through low-dimensional noise-driven transitions, producing right-skewed dwell-time distributions matching empirical data.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 establish attractor types with citations. C24-C29 describe the metastable attractor model for M2, supported by Figure 3 and citations to Recanatesi et al., 2022. The model predictions (C28-C29) are confirmed by data. C30 provides theoretical interpretation supported by citations. The integration of theory and data is well-supported.

results.result: Causal tests of the attractor hypothesis in freely moving animals are lacking. Mean field theory shows that potential well height is proportional to neuronal gain, and decreased pyramidal cell gain can lead to faster action timing.
results.evaluation: C31 identifies a gap in the literature (appropriate for a review). C32 presents a theoretical result from mean field theory but lacks direct experimental validation. C33 is a theoretical prediction that has not been tested in the freely moving context. These claims represent theoretical predictions requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: Contextual factors modulate action timing: valid expectations accelerate reaction times and improve detection accuracy in auditory tasks (requiring auditory cortex); optogenetic activation of serotonergic neurons prolongs waiting periods; trial history effects (rewarded vs. failed trials) affect subsequent trial latencies and depend on frontal cortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are all supported by citations to experimental work (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011; Fonseca et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2012; Murakami et al., 2014, 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021). These represent well-established experimental findings demonstrating contextual modulation of behavior.

results.result: Changes in baseline input levels modulate transition times between metastable attractors by altering barrier heights, providing a mechanism for contextual modulation of reaction times and sensory coding speed. Gain modulation is a general mechanism for flexible control in motor cortex networks, allowing learning of diverse motor outputs through reward-based training.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by citations to theoretical modeling work (Mazzucato et al., 2019; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021) and experimental data (Samuelsen et al., 2012). C42-C43 are supported by citation to theoretical work (Stroud et al., 2018). The mechanistic explanation links theory to experimental observations.

results.result: Contextual manipulations affect behavioral sequences by changing state usage and transition probabilities. Monocular vs. binocular mice show different strategies in distance estimation tasks. Drug administration can be predicted from behavioral patterns with high accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by citation and Figure 5A data (Parker et al., 2021). C46 is stated as a general observation from experimental studies. C47 is supported by citation to Wiltschko et al., 2020. These demonstrate contextual effects on behavioral sequences.

results.result: Computational models of corticostriatal circuits can generate flexible behavioral sequences. The basal ganglia sequentially disinhibit thalamic units triggering motif execution via thalamocortical loops. Sequential patterns can be learned through biologically plausible plasticity, with fast cortical and slow subcortical learning enabling gradual transfer of behavioral control.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by citations to modeling work (Logiaco et al., 2021; Murray and Escola, 2017) and experimental work (Kawai et al., 2015). These represent theoretical models with biological plausibility supported by experimental evidence of learning-execution dissociation.

results.result: In the Marshmallow task, approximately 10% of temporal variability in waiting times is attributable to trial history effects (medial prefrontal cortex-dependent), while the remaining 90% is attributed to stochastic mechanisms likely originating from metastable dynamics.
results.evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations to experimental work (C51: Murakami et al., 2017) and modeling work (C52: Recanatesi et al., 2022). The quantitative decomposition of variability sources is based on empirical data and provides evidence for the stochastic component of behavioral variability.

results.result: C. elegans locomotor behavior exhibits a clear three-level hierarchical organization (sub-second body-bends/head-casts, second-long crawling, slow reverse-forward cycles). This hierarchy is generated by nested neuronal dynamics where slow activity across many neurons supports upper-level programs while fast local dynamics drive lower-level behaviors, forming a tree-like structure. State-level hierarchy may rely on neuromodulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by citations to experimental work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hallinen et al., 2021) and Figure 6. C56 is an inference from the data structure. C57 is supported by citations (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Flavell et al., 2013) but marked as speculation. The C. elegans case provides strong evidence for hierarchical organization.

results.result: Fruit fly behavior exhibits a hierarchical organization with ~100 stereotyped actions. Information bottleneck analysis reveals multiple timescales organized hierarchically, with non-Markovian structure on longer timescales and a tree-like, nonoverlapping structure where actions are segregated by activity type. Individual flies show variability in high-level temporal structure linked to specific genes and neural activity in the central complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by citations to experimental work (Berman et al., 2014, 2016; Cande et al., 2018; Tao et al., 2019; Ayroles et al., 2014; Buchanan et al., 2015) and Figure 7A. The fly behavioral hierarchy is well-characterized through multiple complementary approaches including optogenetics and genetics.

results.result: Rodent behavioral hierarchy shows hierarchical learning (not sequential) in the 'penguin dance' task, with striatal pathways differentially controlling action expression vs. subsequence switching. Multiscale analysis reveals non-Markovian dynamics peaking at 10-100s timescales, with pattern sequences at 15s and arousal states at minute-long timescales. Fragile X mutant rats show abnormal grooming with different sequences/states. Individual differences are more pronounced at longer timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by citation to Geddes et al., 2018 with experimental data. C67-C69 describe findings from Marshall et al., 2021. C70 is supported by Figure 7C data. C71 is supported by citation to Marshall et al., 2021. These provide evidence for hierarchical organization in rodents, though the structure may differ from flies.

results.result: Neural activity exhibits heterogeneous timescales across species and brain areas. In zebrafish and primate brainstem, decay times vary from 0.5-50s. Primate frontal areas encode reward history over 10 trials with power-law distribution. Within-area autocorrelation timescales are right-skewed and lognormal (10ms-1s), with hierarchical structure across cortical areas (50-350ms occipital-to-frontal). Freely moving rodent M2/prefrontal cortex shows multiple timescales from sub-second to minutes. Hippocampus encodes multiplexed information across multiple trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 are supported by citations to experimental work (Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013; Bernacchia et al., 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022; McKenzie et al., 2014) and Figures 8A-C. This provides strong evidence for temporal heterogeneity in neural activity.

results.result: Multiple computational mechanisms can generate heterogeneous timescales: single-cell biophysical properties (sub-second range), recurrent networks at criticality or with symmetric couplings (longer timescales), and networks with functional clusters and heterogeneous couplings. Linear networks with local assemblies and spatial heterogeneity reproduce experimental data. In clustered networks, timescale is proportional to cluster size, yielding distributions matching cortical observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 are supported by citations to theoretical work (Gjorgjieva et al., 2016; Toyoizumi and Abbott, 2011; Magnasco et al., 2009; Martí et al., 2018; Stern et al., 2021) and experimental work (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Kiani et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014). The progression from simple to complex mechanisms is well-supported, with models reproducing experimental findings (C86, Figure 8).

results.result: No study has investigated temporal hierarchies in neural activity during naturalistic behavior, though necessary tools (chronic recordings, pose tracking) are now available.
results.evaluation: C88 identifies a clear gap in the literature (appropriate for a review). C89 is supported by citations to recent methodological advances (Juavinett et al., 2019; van Daal et al., 2021; Mathis et al., 2018; Marshall et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2019). This correctly identifies an important future direction.

results.result: The 'Attractors all the way down' framework proposes that behavioral units at all hierarchical levels (actions, sequences, activities) are represented by metastable attractors. Stochasticity arises from low-dimensional variability in mesoscopic feedback loops. Average transition times depend on barrier heights, which increase up the hierarchy. Larger neural populations encode slower features via nested cluster architecture. Contextual modulations operate via gain modulation of barrier heights.
results.evaluation: C90 is supported by citations to experimental work. C91-C96 represent a proposed theoretical framework extending from established findings. While C90 has experimental support, C91-C96 are largely speculative extensions (marked as SPECULATION/INFERENCE in evidence_type). The framework is logically coherent and builds on established principles, but lacks direct experimental validation for the hierarchical extension. This is appropriate for a review proposing future directions, but the speculative nature limits support.

results.result: The hierarchical attractor framework predicts: (1) neurons exhibit conjunctive selectivity to multiple hierarchical levels, (2) single-cell activity is modulated by many attractors (dense coding), and (3) single-neuron fluctuations vary over multiple timescales simultaneously. These predictions are supported by observations in rodent hippocampus, primate prefrontal cortex, sensory/frontal areas, and C. elegans.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 present predictions from the theoretical framework that are supported by citations to experimental work (McKenzie et al., 2014; Rigotti et al., 2013; Mazzucato et al., 2015; Recanatesi et al., 2022; Kaplan et al., 2020) and Figure 6. The predictions are testable and have empirical support, though not all in the context of naturalistic behavior.

results.result: Fly behavioral hierarchy approximates a tree structure where lower-level actions only occur during specific higher-level activities. This can be modeled by hierarchical Hopfield networks. However, the mammalian hierarchy may not be tree-like (Marshall et al., 2021 results), potentially allowing flexible motor element reuse across sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by citation to Berman et al., 2016 and Figure 7. C102-C103 are supported by citation to theoretical work (Parga and Virasoro, 1986). C104-C105 acknowledge uncertainty about mammalian hierarchy structure, supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2021 and modeling work (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco and Escola, 2020; Logiaco et al., 2021; Geddes et al., 2018). The distinction between fly and mammalian hierarchies is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Flexible behavioral sequences can be generated and learned in cortico-thalamic-basal ganglia models through rearranging motifs and biologically plausible Hebbian plasticity. In mammals, M2 generates metastable attractors for actions, while subcortical areas (basal ganglia, thalamus) are involved in sequence generation. M2 neurons show mixed selectivity. Behavioral units are encoded as cortical attractors while transitions rely on cortico-subcortical feedback loops.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by citations to modeling work (Logiaco et al., 2021; Murray and Escola, 2017). C108-C109 are supported by citations to experimental work (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022) and modeling work (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021). C110 is supported by citations (Recanatesi et al., 2022; Rigotti et al., 2013). C111 is stated as a hypothesis but supported by citations to modeling work. The integration of experimental and theoretical work is well-supported.

results.result: During social interactions like courtship, flies can simultaneously perform behaviors (locomotion and singing) that would be mutually exclusive in isolation. This suggests the tree-like hierarchical organization observed in isolated individuals might break down during social interactions, leading to flexible organization where actions are shared between sequences.
results.evaluation: C112 is stated as established knowledge about fly courtship behavior. C113 is a logical inference from C112 and the tree-like structure established earlier. While speculative, this represents a reasonable hypothesis about how social context might alter behavioral organization. The claim is appropriately framed as speculation.

results.result: Temporal variability in behavior includes contextual effects (faster reaction times when stimuli are expected), stochastic components (right-skewed movement duration distributions), and potential sources from motor periphery (muscle force noise) or deterministic chaos in neural activity/biomechanics.
results.evaluation: C5 is supported by citation to Jaramillo and Zador, 2011. C6 is supported by citations to multiple studies (Wiltschko et al., 2015; Findley et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022). C7 is supported by citations to studies investigating motor variability sources (van Beers et al., 2004; Costa et al., 2021; Loveless et al., 2019). These establish the multiple sources of temporal variability.
